title: Earth's Early History
seo_title: Earth's History Worksheets: Radiometric Dating, Meteorites and Early Earth (Earth Science)
standard_text: Apply scientific reasoning and evidence from ancient Earth materials, meteorites, and other planetary surfaces to construct an account of Earth's formation and early history.
meta_desc: Free high school Earth and space science worksheets on Earth's early history (NGSS HS-ESS1-6): radiometric dating, half-lives, meteorites, zircons, Moon rocks and craters. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
key_sub: Meteorites, zircons and Moon rocks, dated by radioactive decay, tell Earth's early story.
body_html:
How to think about it

Old materials and other worlds record Earth's early history.

  • Radiometric dating: after n half-lives, (1/2)n of the parent is left. Parent : daughter 1 : 1 → 1 half-life; 1 : 3 → 2; 1 : 7 → 3.
  • Meteorites date the solar system (~4.56 billion years). Zircons, Moon rocks and craters show early crust, a giant impact and heavy bombardment.
  • Choose an isotope whose half-life fits the age you want to measure.
Example

1/4 of potassium-40 left (half-life 1.25 billion years)?

2 half-lives

2 × 1.25

Answer: 2.5 billion years

Example

Parent : daughter = 1 : 3?

1/4 left = 2 half-lives

Answer: 2 half-lives

Common mistakes

  • Thinking nothing is left after two half-lives.
  • Using carbon-14 to date dinosaur bones.
  • Thinking the oldest rocks give Earth's exact age.

faq.q: How do scientists know Earth's age?
faq.a: Radiometric dating of meteorites and Moon rocks, which formed with the solar system and were not recycled, gives about 4.56 billion years.
A radioactive parent isotope decays into a daughter at a known half-life. The fraction of parent left tells how many half-lives have passed.

faq.q: Why use different isotopes for different ages?
faq.a: The half-life should be similar to the age being measured so a measurable amount of parent and daughter remains.

c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago.

items.q: Why are meteorites used to find Earth's age?

items.q: Why can't carbon-14 date dinosaur fossils?
